title: Haemothorax
subject: Surgery
summary: Blood accumulates in the pleural space after trauma or other causes, compromising lung expansion. Prompt recognition, drainage and control of bleeding are essential, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Diagnosed by chest X‑ray (opaque hemithorax, meniscus sign) or bedside ultrasound (fluid with low echogenicity).
CT scan confirms volume and source when available.

sections.p: Severity is graded by volume and hemodynamic impact.
In low‑resource East African hospitals, trauma dominates, but other local causes must be considered.
b: Blunt chest trauma (road‑traffic accidents, falls).
Penetrating injury (stab, gunshot).
Rib fracture with intercostal vessel tear.
Iatrogenic (central line, thoracentesis).
Tuberculosis pleural erosion (rare).
Coagulopathy from severe malaria, HIV‑related thrombocytopenia.

sections.p: Patients present with chest pain, dyspnoea and signs of reduced breath sounds on the affected side.
b: Dullness to percussion, decreased tactile fremitus.
Reduced or absent breath sounds, egophony may be lost.
Tracheal shift away if massive.
Hypotension, tachycardia if bleeding is significant.

t.b: Confirms presence and approximate volume of fluid; opaque hemithorax suggests large haemothorax.
Detects fluid quickly at bedside; useful when X‑ray unavailable.
Shows falling haemoglobin indicating ongoing bleed; watch for anemia.
Identifies coagulopathy that may worsen bleeding; correct before invasive procedures.
Maps source of bleed, assesses associated injuries; not mandatory for initial management.

sections.p: Uncontrolled bleeding can lead to shock, respiratory failure and fibrothorax.
b: Persistent hypotension despite fluids.
Increasing chest tube output >200 mL/hr for 3 hrs.
Development of empyema if blood is not evacuated.
Fibrothorax causing restrictive lung disease.

sections.p: Control bleeding, evacuate blood, and support respiration.
b: Immediate large‑bore (28‑32 Fr) intercostal chest drain with underwater seal.
Fluid resuscitation with crystalloids; give blood products if available.
Correct coagulopathy with fresh frozen plasma or vitamin K.
Analgesia (opioids or NSAIDs) to allow deep breathing; avoid NSAIDs if coagulopathic.

sections.p: Monitor drainage, lung re‑expansion and signs of infection.
b: Serial chest X‑rays until lung fully expands.
Remove chest tube when output <100 mL/24 h and lung is expanded.
Vaccinate against pneumococcus and influenza in chronic cases.
Educate on injury prevention (road safety, protective gear).

sections.p: Conditions that also cause a fluid‑filled hemithorax.
b: Pleural effusion (serous fluid, not blood).
Empyema (pus, thick fluid, often febrile).
Pneumothorax (air, hyperresonant percussion).

sections.p: Certain findings may mask a haemothorax.
b: Small haemothorax may appear normal on supine X‑ray; use ultrasound.
Coexisting pulmonary contusion can cause infiltrates that mimic haemorrhage.
Low output from chest tube does not rule out ongoing bleed if clotting occurs.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden drop in blood pressure or heart rate >120 bpm.
Chest tube output >200 mL/hr for 3 hrs.
Increasing dyspnoea with oxygen saturation <90% despite supplemental O₂.

faq.q: Why is a large‑bore chest tube preferred?
faq.a: It allows rapid evacuation of thick blood and prevents tube blockage.

faq.q: Can a haemothorax resolve without surgery?
faq.a: Small to moderate cases often resolve after drainage; massive or clotted haemothorax needs thoracotomy.

faq.q: What is the difference between haemothorax and empyema on ultrasound?
faq.a: Haemothorax appears anechoic or low‑level echoes; empyema shows complex septated fluid with higher echogenicity.

exam: How would you differentiate a haemothorax from a simple pleural effusion on a supine chest X‑ray? — Haamothorax shows a homogenous opacity with a meniscus sign and possible mediastinal shift; effusion may be more lateral and less dense.
Why should NSAIDs be avoided in a patient with a haemothorax and coagulopathy? — NSAIDs impair platelet function, worsening bleeding.

Explain the pathophysiological reason for tracheal deviation away from a massive haemothorax. — Accumulated blood exerts pressure, pushing the mediastinum to the opposite side, compromising ventilation.

In a resource‑limited setting without CT, how can you identify the source of bleeding? — Use bedside ultrasound to locate fluid and assess for active bleeding, correlate with external wounds and rib fractures.
